..
As of 156 PM EST Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Current radar depicts our parent surface low occluding 
over western Pennsylvania this afternoon, with RAP surface analysis 
denoting the secondary coastal low beginning to deepen near the 
Delaware Bay. This secondary low will become the dominant system 
tonight into tomorrow with the better forcing and dynamics focused 
to our south. Models continue to shunt the best moisture profiles to 
our south where an axis of stronger frontogenesis looks to set up 
along Long Island to Cape Cod. That said, overrunning precipitation 
has already overspread much of southern Vermont this afternoon with 
road cameras showing snow falling across our higher elevations in 
the southern Greens, mainly above 1500ft. However, below 1500ft, 
into the area valleys, rain is expected to remain the dominant ptype 
through much of this event. Drier air along the International Border 
is helping to stifle much of the northward moisture extent, with 
precipitation amount trends lowering for areas north of US-2, and 
have since cut back on PoPs for these areas. Total snow amounts have 
come down slightly in the mountains with generally 2 to 4 inches, 
heavily tied to the terrain. A Winter Weather Advisory remains in 
effect until 10 AM Friday for eastern Addison and Rutland Counties 
in Vermont, as well as western Essex County in New York. 

Into tonight, with the combination of dynamical cooling and 
nighttime cooling, some flakes may be able to mix into the the lower 
elevations like the Champlain and Connecticut River Valleys. Though 
surface temperatures in the aforementioned areas will remain at or 
just above freezing, limiting any accumulations to mainly just 
grassy surfaces. As the low continues to track east Friday, cyclonic 
north to northwest flow will develop and keep snow showers in the 
mountains as upslope snow.

KEY MESSAGE 2: North to northwest cyclonic flow will keep moisture 
wrapping around the coast low late Friday through early Sunday. As 
boundary layer temperatures cool with cold advection towards late 
Friday, orographic lift will help sustain snow showers in the 
upslope favored western facing slopes of the central and northern 
Greens and Adirondacks. In addition, with lake temperatures becoming 
10C warmer than the advective cold air aloft, narrow lake enhanced 
snow showers may develop downstream of Lake Champlain overnight 
Friday and during the day Saturday. Areas that may see some 
additional rain/snow enhancement look to be in the areas along a 
line from Shelburne to Lincoln. The exact placement and actual 
development of such a mesoscale lake streamer are still uncertain, 
but dynamically this synoptic setup is favorable for Lake clouds and 
subsequent precipitation enhancement. Precipitation totals would be 
light in the aforementioned areas, with mainly rain northwest of 
Bristol, and perhaps some locally enhanced snow showers around an 
inch of snow near Bristol, Lincoln, and the Ripton areas. 

Outside of the Lake enhanced showers, blocked flow will lead to snow 
showers along areas in eastern Chittenden and Franklin Counties in 
Vermont, and northern Franklin and eastern St. Lawrence Counties in 
New York. This second round of wintry weather looks to be more 
favorable for accumulations for our area, with snow levels hovering 
around 1000ft, and better dynamics. There is the potential for a 
mesoband to develop out of Ontario, with decent frontogenesis, and 
associated 50 to 100J/kg of cape in the Champlain Valley Saturday 
morning. If it materializes, brief accumulations are possible down 
to the valley floors due to dynamical cooling and an additional 
couple inches would be possible across the higher terrain. However, 
this should not significantly change the impacts. Any snow in the 
lower valleys would mainly be a coating to a slushy wet snow at this 
time. At this point, the snowfall looks too light to cause power 
outages but far southern Vermont will have to be watched in case the 
mesoband comes in and stalls there for a couple hours. The shortwave 
responsible for the upslope snow will swing south and exit the area 
late Sunday, with generally drying conditions by Monday morning.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Model consensus remains strong with little spread
showing high pressure building across the Northeast next week.
Most models support the ridge axis deflecting systems along a
more northward track in central to northern Canadian latitudes.
This will allow for some drying and warming through the week
with highs generally in the 50s for most locations by 
Wednesday and most lows in the upper 20s to lower 30s. With 
ideal conditions for radiational cooling being likely, colder 
overnight temperatures should be anticipated for the usual 
colder hollows.
